claim: Splicing is the stepwise molecular process by which introns are removed from pre-mRNA and exons are joined together to form mature mRNA sequences.
source: Splicing is the stepwise molecular process by which introns are removed from pre-mRNA and exons are joined together to form mature mRNA sequences.
evidence: This is a definition statement that draws from established scientific knowledge about splicing.

claim: Some work suggests that splicing occurs very shortly after the RNA polymerase transcribes a particular splice junction.
source: Some work suggests that splicing occurs very shortly after the RNA polymerase transcribes a particular splice junction (Beyer et al., 1981; Oesterreich et al., 2016; Khodor et al., 2011; Reimer et al., 2021)
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: Other work suggests that many pre-mRNA are fully transcribed before splicing occurs.
source: while other work suggests that many pre-mRNA are fully transcribed before splicing occurs (Tsai et al., 1980; Drexler et al., 2020; Coulon et al., 2014; Khodor et al., 2012; Choquet et al., 2022)
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: Pre-mRNA formed clouds around the transcription site at super-resolution levels.
source: At super-resolution levels, we found that pre-mRNA formed clouds around the transcription site.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from expansion microscopy experiments.

claim: These clouds indicate the existence of a transcription-site-proximal zone through which RNA move more slowly than in the nucleoplasm.
source: These clouds indicate the existence of a transcription-site-proximal zone through which RNA move more slowly than in the nucleoplasm.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the observation of clouds around transcription sites.

claim: Full-length pre-mRNA undergo continuous splicing as they move through this zone following transcription.
source: Full-length pre-mRNA undergo continuous splicing as they move through this zone following transcription
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental observations from expansion microscopy and RNA FISH.

claim: Splicing can occur post-transcriptionally but still within the proximity of the transcription site, thus seeming co-transcriptional by most assays.
source: suggesting a model in which splicing can occur post-transcriptionally but still within the proximity of the transcription site, thus seeming co-transcriptional by most assays.
evidence: This is a model proposed based on the experimental findings.

claim: At least one intron of each observed endogenous gene is spliced post-transcriptionally.
source: At least one intron of each observed endogenous gene is spliced post-transcriptionally
evidence: This claim is supported by RNA FISH data showing dispersed pre-mRNA for all tested genes.

claim: For the genes CPS1, EEF2, TM4SF1, and FKBP5, at least one intron was present in dispersed pre-mRNA in both transformed cell lines (HeLa and A549) and non-transformed cells (CRL-2097).
source: We found that for the genes CPS1, EEF2, TM4SF1, and FKBP5, at least one intron was present in dispersed pre-mRNA in both transformed cell lines (HeLa and A549) and non-transformed cells (CRL-2097) (three to five introns tested per gene, Figure 1D)
evidence: This claim is supported by RNA FISH data shown in Figure 1D.

claim: Pre-mRNA dispersal is a generic feature of transcription and splicing that is not dependent on the particular cell line used.
source: suggesting that pre-mRNA dispersal is a generic feature of transcription and splicing that is not dependent on the particular cell line used.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from observing dispersal in multiple cell lines.

claim: The dispersal patterns for any one particular intron were not necessarily consistent between HeLa and CRL-2097 cells.
source: However, we found that the dispersal patterns for any one particular intron were not necessarily consistent between HeLa and CRL-2097 cells, suggesting splicing patterns may be influenced by cellular context.
evidence: This claim is supported by RNA FISH data comparing different cell lines.

claim: Splicing patterns may be influenced by cellular context.
source: suggesting splicing patterns may be influenced by cellular context.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from observing different dispersal patterns in different cell lines.

claim: Pre-mRNA contain fewer introns as they increase in distance from the transcription site.
source: However, we do note that pre-mRNA contain fewer introns as they increase in distance from the transcription site (Figure 1—figure supplement 2D)
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2D.

claim: Pulse-chase experiments have shown that the 'yield' of splicing events is high for mRNA.
source: Furthermore, pulse-chase experiments have shown that the 'yield' of splicing events is high for mRNA, suggesting that most pre-mRNA do not go down a dead-end pathway (Eser et al., 2016; Wachutka et al., 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: Most pre-mRNA do not go down a dead-end pathway.
source: suggesting that most pre-mRNA do not go down a dead-end pathway (Eser et al., 2016; Wachutka et al., 2019).
evidence: This is an inference drawn from cited pulse-chase experiments.

claim: Splicing of different introns within the same primary transcript can occur in any order.
source: Overall, our data support a model in which splicing of different introns within the same primary transcript can occur in any order.
evidence: This claim is supported by data showing various patterns of splicing intermediates.

claim: Lack of ordering between introns did not depend on distance between them.
source: Lack of ordering between introns did not depend on distance between them, with no ordering observed for the neighboring EEF2 introns 1 and 2 as well as the distant CSP1 introns 1 and 34.
evidence: This claim is supported by data from RNA FISH experiments.

claim: Transcripts are untethered to the transcription site and move through a slow-moving transcription-site-proximal zone where splicing occurs after transcription is completed.
source: Transcripts are untethered to the transcription site and move through a slow-moving transcription-site-proximal zone where splicing occurs after transcription is completed
evidence: This claim is supported by expansion microscopy and live-cell imaging data.

claim: The 5', 3', and middle intron probe signals formed small clouds where we had previously observed the tight transcriptional focus.
source: Upon expanding, labeling, and imaging, we indeed observed that the 5', 3', and middle intron probe signals formed small clouds where we had previously observed the tight transcriptional focus (Figure 2C, quantified in Figure 2—figure supplement 2C).
evidence: This claim is supported by expansion microscopy data shown in Figure 2C.

claim: The expanded transcription site contains multiple 3' and 5' spots, while expanded cytoplasmic mRNA contain one 3' and 5' spot.
source: Of note, the expanded transcription site contains multiple 3' and 5' spots, while expanded cytoplasmic mRNA contain one 3' and 5' spot, indicating the presence of multiple transcripts at the transcription site as opposed to a single transcript broken into multiple parts as a result of expansion (Figure 2B).
evidence: This claim is supported by expansion microscopy data shown in Figure 2B.

claim: The predicted concentration (18 molecules per cubic micron) was far lower than the actual concentration (235 molecules per cubic micron) in the vicinity of the transcription site measured by expansion microscopy.
source: We found that the predicted concentration (18 molecules per cubic micron) was far lower than the actual concentration (235 molecules per cubic micron) in the vicinity of the transcription site measured by expansion microscopy (Figure 2E).
evidence: This claim is supported by quantitative analysis of expansion microscopy data.

claim: This high concentration in the 'cloud' is not consistent with free diffusion subsequent to the completion of transcription.
source: This high concentration in the 'cloud' is not consistent with free diffusion subsequent to the completion of transcription (Figure 2D scenario II)
evidence: This is an inference drawn from comparing observed concentrations to a diffusion model.

claim: The high concentration in the cloud is compatible with the existence of a distinct 'proximal zone' surrounding the transcription site through which pre-mRNA move more slowly than in the more distant nucleoplasm.
source: but is compatible with the existence of a distinct 'proximal zone' surrounding the transcription site through which pre-mRNA move more slowly than in the more distant nucleoplasm (Figure 2D scenario I).
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the observed concentration data.

claim: We observed similarly sized clouds for both the 5' and 3' ends of the pre-mRNA in the proximal zone.
source: We observed similarly sized clouds for both the 5' and 3' ends of the pre-mRNA in the proximal zone.
evidence: This claim is supported by expansion microscopy data.

claim: The diameter of the cylindrical slow-moving zone around the gene body is around 0.3 µm.
source: Based on the size of these clouds, we estimated the diameter of this cylindrical slow-moving zone around the gene body to be around 0.3 µm (Figure 2F, see Materials and methods for calculations).
evidence: This claim is supported by quantitative analysis of expansion microscopy data.

claim: This width does not depend on the length of an individual transcript or gene body, but rather extends radially outward from the gene body.
source: This width does not depend on the length of an individual transcript or gene body, but rather extends radially outward from the gene body.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the observation that clouds are similar in size for different regions.

claim: A large proportion of the splicing occurs post-transcriptionally while the pre-mRNA were moving through the proximal zone.
source: We concluded that pre-mRNA are not spliced immediately upon transcription, but rather that a large proportion of the splicing occurs post-transcriptionally while the pre-mRNA were moving through the proximal zone.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from expansion microscopy data.

claim: The intronic signal also formed a cloud, showing that splicing has not yet been completed as the pre-mRNA move through this proximal zone.
source: Similar to the signals from the 5' and 3' ends, the intronic signal also formed a cloud, showing that splicing has not yet been completed as the pre-mRNA move through this proximal zone (Figure 2G and H).
evidence: This claim is supported by expansion microscopy data shown in Figure 2G and H.

claim: The clouds of the 5' and 3' ends of the pre-mRNA are typically non-overlapping and are further apart than the mature mRNA we found in the cytoplasm.
source: Furthermore, the clouds of the 5' and 3' ends of the pre-mRNA are typically non-overlapping and are further apart than the mature mRNA we found in the cytoplasm, suggesting that these clouds do not represent fully mature, spliced mRNA (Figure 2I).
evidence: This claim is supported by expansion microscopy data shown in Figure 2I.

claim: The majority of images (141 of 205) showed evidence of substantial eccentricity (defined as eccentricity >0.6).
source: We found that the majority of images (141 of 205) showed evidence of substantial eccentricity (defined as eccentricity >0.6) (Figure 3C).
evidence: This claim is supported by quantitative analysis of live-cell imaging data shown in Figure 3C.

claim: RNA were likely retained at the site for some time following transcription.
source: As these sites are unambiguously larger than a diffraction limited spot, we concluded that RNA were likely retained at the site for some time following transcription, corroborating the existence of the slow-moving zone.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the observation of eccentric transcription sites in live-cell imaging.

claim: The relative positions of the 5', 3', and middle intron clouds adopted a wide variety of conformations.
source: Similarly, in our expansion microscopy data, the relative positions of the 5', 3', and middle intron clouds adopted a wide variety of conformations, suggesting that the linear genomic order of the pre-mRNA may not be strictly maintained during transit through the proximal zone (Figure 2C).
evidence: This claim is supported by expansion microscopy data shown in Figure 2C.

claim: The linear genomic order of the pre-mRNA may not be strictly maintained during transit through the proximal zone.
source: suggesting that the linear genomic order of the pre-mRNA may not be strictly maintained during transit through the proximal zone (Figure 2C).
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the observation of varied conformations of clouds.

claim: The length of each intron, as well as the strength of its 3' and 5' splice site, did not affect its dispersal from the transcription site.
source: The length of each intron, as well as the strength of its 3' and 5' splice site, did not affect its dispersal from the transcription site, suggesting that transcript size and splice site sequence are not major contributors to the dynamics of the slow-moving zone (Figure 2—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 3.

claim: Transcript size and splice site sequence are not major contributors to the dynamics of the slow-moving zone.
source: suggesting that transcript size and splice site sequence are not major contributors to the dynamics of the slow-moving zone (Figure 2—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the observation that intron length and splice site strength do not affect dispersal.

claim: Neither the 5' exon nor 3' exon signals overlapped with actively elongating RNA polymerase II immunofluorescence signals.
source: Also, neither the 5' exon nor 3' exon signals overlapped with actively elongating RNA polymerase II immunofluorescence signals (see Materials and methods)
evidence: This claim is supported by immunofluorescence data.

claim: The relatively few mRNA spots that are quite close to RNA polymerase II signal are undergoing active transcription, while the majority of pre-mRNA in the slow-moving proximal zone are not being actively transcribed.
source: potentially suggesting the relatively few mRNA spots that are quite close to RNA polymerase II signal are undergoing active transcription, while the majority of pre-mRNA in the slow-moving proximal zone are not being actively transcribed (Figure 2G).
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the lack of overlap between exon signals and polymerase II signals.

claim: The size of 5', intron, and 3' clouds, the number of spots in each cloud, and the area of live-cell transcription sites varied considerably from cell to cell.
source: Another interesting observation was that the size of 5', intron, and 3' clouds, the number of spots in each cloud, and the area of live-cell transcription sites varied considerably from cell to cell (Figures 2C, H, 3A, B).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figures 2C, H, 3A, B.

claim: Upon splicing inhibition, we observed three distinct trafficking behaviors for pre-mRNA species: nuclear dispersal, blobs, and non-splicing inhibited.
source: Upon splicing inhibition, we observed three distinct trafficking behaviors for pre-mRNA species: one in which there are increased numbers of dispersed pre-mRNA throughout the nucleus (nuclear dispersal; consistent with scenario 1), one in which the pre-mRNA are located in a large blob, likely around the transcription-site-proximal zone or another nuclear body (blobs; scenario 2 or 3), and one in which the pre-mRNA dispersal pattern looked identical with or without splicing inhibition (non-splicing inhibited) (Figure 4B and C).
evidence: This claim is supported by RNA FISH data after splicing inhibition shown in Figure 4B and C.

claim: The compartmentalization pattern only appeared for 3 out of the 16 genes we tested (EEF2, GAPDH, and RPL13A).
source: The compartmentalization pattern only appeared for 3 out of the 16 genes we tested (EEF2, GAPDH, and RPL13A), whereas we observed a nuclear dispersal phenotype for 7 genes and no change in dispersal for 6 genes.
evidence: This claim is supported by RNA FISH data after splicing inhibition.

claim: The 5' and 3' ends of the pre-mRNA both filled the entire blob, suggesting that the pre-mRNA spread to fill the entire putative compartment.
source: We found, however, that the 5' and 3' ends of the pre-mRNA both filled the entire blob, suggesting that the pre-mRNA spread to fill the entire putative compartment (as in scenario 3 described above, compartmentalization) (Figure 4A and D).
evidence: This claim is supported by RNA FISH data shown in Figure 4A and D.

claim: These compartmentalized pre-mRNA did indeed appear near nuclear speckles both before and after splicing inhibition.
source: To test this hypothesis, we performed RNA FISH simultaneously with immunofluorescence for SC35, a component of speckles, and saw that these compartmentalized pre-mRNA did indeed appear near nuclear speckles both before (Figure 4—figure supplement 1C) and after (Figure 4G) splicing inhibition.
evidence: This claim is supported by combined RNA FISH and immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 4G and Figure 4—figure supplement 1C.

claim: The genes that localized to compartments post-splicing inhibitor treatment were indeed the closest to speckles.
source: We found that even in the absence of pladeinolide B, the genes that localized to compartments post-splicing inhibitor treatment were indeed the closest to speckles.
evidence: This claim is supported by analysis of TSA-Seq 2.0 data and RNA FISH data.

claim: Multiple introns retained in pre-mRNA from the same gene colocalized to the same subset of speckles.
source: We observed that multiple introns retained in pre-mRNA from the same gene colocalized to the same subset of speckles (Figure 4E)
evidence: This claim is supported by RNA FISH data shown in Figure 4E.

claim: Pre-mRNA from multiple 'compartmentalization' genes (EEF2, GAPDH, and RPL13A) localize to a similar set of speckles after splicing inhibition.
source: We also observed that pre-mRNA from multiple 'compartmentalization' genes (EEF2, GAPDH, and RPL13A) localize to a similar set of speckles after splicing inhibition (Figure 4F)
evidence: This claim is supported by RNA FISH data shown in Figure 4F.

claim: mRNA trafficking upon leaving the slow-moving zone is gene specific.
source: Overall, our results suggest that mRNA trafficking upon leaving the slow-moving zone is gene specific.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from observing different trafficking behaviors for different genes.

claim: We saw an increase in both exon and intron spot counts over time and a corresponding increase in the dispersal of some, but not all, introns.
source: We saw an increase in both exon and intron spot counts (Figure 5B) over time and a corresponding increase in the dispersal of some, but not all, introns (Figure 5C).
evidence: This claim is supported by RNA FISH data over a time course shown in Figure 5B and C.

claim: The fact that intron dispersal increased with transcription level for at least some introns shows that dispersal is not an inherent property of each intron but can depend on other variables like the level of transcription.
source: The fact that intron dispersal increased with transcription level for at least some introns shows that dispersal is not an inherent property of each intron but can depend on other variables like the level of transcription (Figure 5C).
evidence: This is an inference drawn from observing increased dispersal with increased transcription.

claim: Intron 9 did not exhibit an increase in dispersal even with long exposure to dexamethasone (8 hr).
source: Intron 9 did not exhibit an increase in dispersal even with long exposure to dexamethasone (8 hr) (Figure 5C).
evidence: This claim is supported by RNA FISH data shown in Figure 5C.

claim: We observed a significant increase in the proportion of intron signal for two introns over time (from 0% to 22% for intron 1 and from 0% to 29% for intron 8).
source: Instead, we observed a significant increase in the proportion of intron signal for two introns over time (from 0% to 22% for intron 1 and from 0% to 29% for intron 8; Figure 5D)
evidence: This claim is supported by quantitative analysis of RNA FISH data shown in Figure 5D.

claim: The increased dispersal of some introns during periods of increased transcription may be due to a local depletion of splicing factors.
source: We hypothesized that the increased dispersal of some introns during periods of increased transcription may be due to a local depletion of splicing factors.
evidence: This is a hypothesis proposed to explain the observed increase in dispersal with increased transcription.

claim: Even the same intron can exhibit a range of spatiotemporal patterns of splicing depending on expression levels and potentially on limiting splicing factors in the vicinity of the gene itself.
source: These increases in the percent of distal post-transcriptional splicing show that even the same intron can exhibit a range of spatiotemporal patterns of splicing depending on expression levels and potentially on limiting splicing factors in the vicinity of the gene itself.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from observing changes in dispersal with transcription level.

claim: Our results support a model that unifies many of the observations made of both co-transcriptional and post-transcriptional splicing.
source: Our results support a model that unifies many of the observations made of both co-transcriptional and post-transcriptional splicing.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the overall findings of the study.

claim: Splicing can occur continuously and post-transcriptionally while pre-mRNA move through this slow-moving zone.
source: We argue that splicing can occur continuously and post-transcriptionally while pre-mRNA move through this slow-moving zone.
evidence: This is a model proposed based on the experimental findings.

claim: Fractionation approaches may have interpreted such splicing intermediates as arising co-transcriptionally owing to proximity to the transcription site.
source: Fractionation approaches may have interpreted such splicing intermediates as arising co-transcriptionally owing to proximity to the transcription site.
evidence: This is an inference about how fractionation methods may have been interpreted.

claim: Our results suggest that pre-mRNA are not tethered to the site of transcription while they move through this transcription-site-proximal compartment.
source: Our results suggest that pre-mRNA are not tethered to the site of transcription while they move through this transcription-site-proximal compartment
evidence: This is an inference drawn from expansion microscopy data showing clouds of 5' and 3' ends.

claim: The lack of colocalization of introns with polymerase II also suggests that splicing is not happening close to polymerase II.
source: The lack of colocalization of introns with polymerase II also suggests that splicing is not happening close to polymerase II.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from immunofluorescence data.

claim: Increased transcription level correlates with intron dispersal.
source: Of note, we see that increased transcription level correlates with intron dispersal, suggesting that the percentage of splicing occurring away from the transcription site is regulated by transcription level for at least some introns.
evidence: This claim is supported by RNA FISH data over a time course of dexamethasone treatment.

claim: The percentage of splicing occurring away from the transcription site is regulated by transcription level for at least some introns.
source: suggesting that the percentage of splicing occurring away from the transcription site is regulated by transcription level for at least some introns.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from observing increased dispersal with increased transcription.

claim: A natural candidate for the slow-moving zone is the chromatin in the vicinity of the gene itself.
source: What might the slow-moving zone represent, physically? A natural candidate is the chromatin in the vicinity of the gene itself.
evidence: This is a speculation about the physical nature of the slow-moving zone.

claim: Live imaging studies have shown that mRNA exhibit slow diffusion in chromatin-dense regions.
source: Live imaging studies have shown that mRNA exhibit slow diffusion in chromatin-dense regions (Vargas et al., 2005).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior work.

claim: Recent work tracking cells over time by sequencing shows that mRNA spends relatively more time on chromatin than in the nucleoplasm.
source: Furthermore, recent work tracking cells over time by sequencing shows that mRNA spends relatively more time on chromatin than in the nucleoplasm (Smalec et al., 2022)
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior work.

claim: The distance between the 5' end and the 3' end of RNA at the site of transcription is greater than the distance between the 5' end and 3' end of mRNA.
source: Our expansion microscopy results suggest that the distance between the 5' end and the 3' end of RNA at the site of transcription is greater than the distance between the 5' end and 3' end of mRNA.
evidence: This claim is supported by expansion microscopy data.

claim: This increased 5' to 3' distance suggests that the transcripts at the site of transcription are either unpackaged (perhaps due to decreased RNA binding proteins occupancy) or are simply longer because there are likely more introns incorporated into the transcripts close to the site of transcription than away from it due to progressive splicing over time.
source: This increased 5' to 3' distance suggests that the transcripts at the site of transcription are either unpackaged (perhaps due to decreased RNA binding proteins occupancy) or are simply longer because there are likely more introns incorporated into the transcripts close to the site of transcription than away from it due to progressive splicing over time.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the observation of increased 5' to 3' distance.

claim: Our results suggest that first come, first serve is not the case, based on seeing low splicing rates (or high dispersion) for even the 5' most introns of some genes.
source: Our results suggest that first come, first serve is not the case, based on seeing low splicing rates (or high dispersion) for even the 5' most introns of some genes.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from RNA FISH data showing dispersal of 5' introns.

claim: Our results also suggest that introns are spliced independently of one another, whether they are genomically proximal or distal to each other.
source: Our results also suggest that introns are spliced independently of one another, whether they are genomically proximal or distal to each other.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from data on splicing intermediates.

claim: The association between specific genes and speckles has been observed before in several studies by Jeanne Lawrence.
source: The association between specific genes and speckles has been observed before in several studies by Jeanne Lawrence (Shopland et al., 2002; Johnson et al., 2000; Smith et al., 1999).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: Our observations are also consistent with those of Girard et al. in which certain genes are retained post-transcriptionally at speckles as splicing occurs and then are released and immediately exported from the nucleus.
source: Our observations are also consistent with those of Girard et al. in which certain genes are retained post-transcriptionally at speckles as splicing occurs and then are released and immediately exported from the nucleus (Girard et al., 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior work and comparison to current findings.

claim: Wang et al. also observed speckle localization of RNA upon microinjection into nuclei.
source: Wang et al. also observed speckle localization of RNA upon microinjection into nuclei (Wang et al., 1991).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior work.

claim: Speckle association can be gene specific and can help retain pre-mRNA in the gene's vicinity until post-transcriptional splicing is completed.
source: Our data further support the conclusion that speckle association can be gene specific and can help retain pre-mRNA in the gene's vicinity until post-transcriptional splicing is completed.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the observed association between specific genes and speckles.

claim: CPS1 was chosen because it is a long and highly expressed gene.
source: CPS1 was chosen because it is a long and highly expressed gene.
evidence: This is a statement about the rationale for gene selection.

claim: EEF2 was chosen because it is a highly expressed housekeeping gene.
source: EEF2 was chosen because it is a highly expressed housekeeping gene.
evidence: This is a statement about the rationale for gene selection.

claim: TM4SF1 was chosen because it is highly expressed and sequencing data suggested it was highly post-transcriptionally spliced.
source: TM4SF1 was chosen because it is highly expressed and sequencing data suggested it was highly post-transcriptionally spliced (see Materials and methods for details).
evidence: This is a statement about the rationale for gene selection based on sequencing data.

claim: FKBP5 was chosen because it is inducible in A549 cells by application of dexamethasone.
source: Finally, FKBP5 was chosen because it is inducible in A549 cells by application of dexamethasone.
evidence: This is a statement about the rationale for gene selection.

claim: We never observed introns in cytoplasmic mRNA, suggesting that all of these introns are eventually spliced out.
source: We never observed introns in cytoplasmic mRNA, suggesting that all of these introns are eventually spliced out (i.e. transcripts with retained introns cannot be exported from the nucleus).
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the absence of introns in cytoplasmic mRNA.

claim: Transcripts with retained introns cannot be exported from the nucleus.
source: (i.e. transcripts with retained introns cannot be exported from the nucleus).
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the absence of introns in cytoplasmic mRNA.

claim: We observed a large range in the number of pre-mRNA observed per cell (from 0 to ~20), which also varied from intron to intron.
source: We observed a large range in the number of pre-mRNA observed per cell (from 0 to ~20), which also varied from intron to intron (Figure 1—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1B.

claim: We found a modest association between splicing index and both mean dispersal and transcription site size.
source: We found a modest association between splicing index and both mean dispersal and transcription site size, suggesting that sequencing of nascent RNA was at least consistent with RNA FISH assessments of distal post-transcriptional splicing
evidence: This claim is supported by comparison of sequencing data and RNA FISH data.

claim: Sequencing of nascent RNA was at least consistent with RNA FISH assessments of distal post-transcriptional splicing.
source: suggesting that sequencing of nascent RNA was at least consistent with RNA FISH assessments of distal post-transcriptional splicing
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the modest association between sequencing and RNA FISH data.

claim: Expansion of transcription sites is isotropic.
source: To confirm isotropic expansion in our system, we imaged the same cell before and after expansion with and without a perturbation that changed the localization of introns (pladeinolide B treatment, which inhibits splicing and causes the introns of EEF2 to form a well-defined blob, see Figure 4) and indeed observed that both the transcription site and the blob of EEF2 introns expanded isotropically (Figure 2—figure supplement 1B, displaying the same cells before and after expansion).
evidence: This claim is supported by imaging the same cells before and after expansion shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1B.

claim: The transcription sites in expanded samples were the same size as those imaged using stochastic optical reconstruction microscopy (STORM).
source: To further ensure that expansion microscopy did not alter the morphology of the transcription site, we confirmed that the transcription sites in expanded samples were the same size as those imaged using stochastic optical reconstruction microscopy (STORM) (Rust et al., 2006), a super-resolution imaging technique that does not rely on expansion (Figure 2—figure supplement 2A and B).
evidence: This claim is supported by comparison of expansion microscopy and STORM data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2A and B.

claim: The 3' and post-3' transcription sites were approximately the same size, suggesting these transcripts are not tethered to chromatin as splicing is occurring.
source: We found that the 3' and post-3' transcription sites were also approximately the same size, suggesting these transcripts are not tethered to chromatin as splicing is occurring (Figure 2—figure supplement 2D and F).
evidence: This claim is supported by RNA FISH data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2D and F.

claim: RNA polymerase II can transcribe beyond the poly-A site.
source: Since RNA polymerase II can transcribe beyond the poly-A site (Anamika et al., 2012; Core et al., 2008)
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: The 3' clouds are consistently larger than the 5' clouds.
source: When the dyes of the two probes are swapped, the 3' clouds are still consistently larger than the 5' clouds, suggesting that it's unlikely to be a dye-bias effect (Figure 2—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: This claim is supported by dye-swap experiments shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1C.

claim: It's unlikely to be a dye-bias effect that 3' clouds are larger than 5' clouds.
source: suggesting that it's unlikely to be a dye-bias effect (Figure 2—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: This is an inference drawn from dye-swap experiments.

claim: In some cases, we observed more 5' spots than 3' spots, which may be due to the interception of an ongoing transcriptional burst.
source: In some cases, we observed more 5' spots than 3' spots, which may be due to the interception of an ongoing transcriptional burst (where RNA polymerase II has already synthesized the 5' ends of the RNA but has not yet synthesized the 3' ends).
evidence: This is a speculation about the reason for observing more 5' spots than 3' spots.

claim: We also observed some cases where there were more 3' spots than 5' spots and indeed many cases where the 3' clouds are more dispersed than the 5' clouds, which may suggest that the spots of 5' probe may represent a pileup of transcripts at the 5' end.
source: We also observed some cases where there were more 3' spots than 5' spots and indeed many cases where the 3' clouds are more dispersed than the 5' clouds, which may suggest that the spots of 5' probe may represent a pileup of transcripts at the 5' end, such that we only see one bright spot where we should see several.
evidence: This is a speculation about the reason for observing more 3' spots than 5' spots.

claim: Varying the colocalization threshold from 0.13 µm (one pixel) to 2.6 µm (20 pixels) did not significantly change dispersal patterns.
source: however, varying this threshold from 0.13 µm (one pixel) to 2.6 µm (20 pixels) did not significantly change dispersal patterns (Figure 1—figure supplement 2A).
evidence: This claim is supported by parameter sweep data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2A.

claim: Intron spots that did not colocalize with an exon spot were presumed to be degradation products or non-specific background and were discarded.
source: Intron spots that did not colocalize with an exon spot were presumed to be degradation products or non-specific background and were discarded (these were generally <25% of intron spots; Supplementary file 1A).
evidence: This is a methodological assumption about non-colocalized intron spots.

claim: We tried several other methods for choosing transcription sites, all of which showed qualitatively similar results.
source: We also tried several other methods for choosing transcription sites, all of which showed qualitatively similar results (Figure 1—figure supplement 1A), showing that the detection of dispersal is not dependent on the choice of method.
evidence: This claim is supported by comparison of different methods shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1A.

claim: The detection of dispersal is not dependent on the choice of method.
